newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania leu outlook hard to predict-central banker.
newsitem.headline: Romania leu outlook hard to predict-central banker.

text.p: An outlook for the Romanian leu currency is hard to predict before presidental run-offs on November 17, which will usher in a new centre-right government, central bank chief economist Daniel Daianu said on Friday.
"It's premature to give a forecast, which depends on an adequate policy mix of the new cabinet," Daianu told Reuters.

Romania's main opposition blocs, which ousted President Ion Iliescu's leftist party in Sunday's general elections, signed a pact on Thursday promising steps to cushion the social impact of reforms, including tighter fiscal and monetary policies.
"We should draw a clear distinction between campaign rhetoric and a serious programme to address the current problems of Romania's economy," Daianu said.

Daianu said the new government would have to tackle urgent measures to make the foreign exchange market operational, which would entail a leu depreciation, while keeping real-positive rates to prevent a run from the leu.

"The key issue will be to impose financial discipline. Otherwise, with rising interest rates, payments arrears will explode," Daianu said, urging steps to cut the bulging state budget deficit, which he said had caused inbalances in the economy in the second half of 1996.

Thursday's pact vowed to blend reforms with welfare. It set down a power-sharing formula in a Convention-led cabinet with former prime minister Petre Roman's Social Democrats, backed by a centre-right parliament majority.

While pledging tax cuts, higher pensions and child benefits and soft loans for farmers and housing, the pact reacts to demands by international lenders, promising to free currency markets, limit the budget deficit and speed up privatisation.

The International Monetary Fund suspended loan tranches for Romania earlier this year after the leftist government curbed the local foreign exchange market, and then eased monetary and fiscal policies in an electoral year.
Inflation is now running at a year-on-year 45 percent, with the country faced with bulging deficits and huge payments arrears almost matching the money supply.
The leu's interbank rates are 30 percent firmer than retail prices, which hover near 4,500 to the dollar.

Daianu anticipated a leu slide with tighter monetary moves: "An adequate policy mix would make the forex market work, which would automatically mean a depreciation." -- Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264
